summary.title: Decision Trees
summary.one_liner: Learn how decision trees pick splits using entropy and information gain (ID3), why single trees are unstable and overfit, and how pruning and random forests help.
keywords: how does a decision tree choose splits
takeaways: Entropy measures how pure or impure a set of labeled samples is: it is zero for a pure node and maximal when classes are evenly mixed.
Information gain, built on entropy, is the criterion the ID3 algorithm uses to choose which rule to split on.
Unpruned trees grow until leaves are pure, which leads to overfitting; pruning via max depth, leaf count, or minimum leaf size helps.
Single decision trees have high variance: small perturbations in training data can produce very different trees.
Ensembles of trees trained on varied data (random forests) reduce this instability.
summary.summary: This interactive MLU-Explain article explains how a decision tree partitions data into regions and how the ID3 algorithm chooses splits. It defines entropy as a measure of impurity, using interactive bubbles to show how entropy changes with class composition, and then links it to information gain. It then discusses the instability and overfitting of unpruned trees, shows the effect of small Gaussian perturbations, and lists pruning strategies. It closes by pointing toward random forests as a way to reduce variance.
